summary: The returned BST must contain one node for every array value, making linear construction time unavoidable. Recursive midpoint splitting creates each node once with logarithmic auxiliary depth.

optimality.argument: Any valid result contains n distinct tree nodes, one for each input value, so constructing it requires Omega(n) time. The current midpoint recursion creates exactly one node per array position and divides into disjoint intervals, giving O(n) total time. Because every split roughly halves its interval, the auxiliary recursion depth is O(log n), excluding the returned nodes.

replacement_checks.evidence: Materializing a BST containing all n distinct input values requires constructing n result nodes.
Each array position belongs to one recursive interval root, so it causes one node construction and no repeated scan or slice.

The source-fidelity-verified examples cover odd and even lengths with multiple accepted balanced shapes; black-box real-test execution verifies every existing ordinary check without inspecting its definition.
